tracks.title: The fork you always end up with
tracks.text: Lesson seven point five — the seam. A deep dive, under wbx. The parent lesson made a bold promise — the same binary, everywhere. Your laptop… your CI box… and the engine's sandbox. And a skeptic is right to doubt it. Cross-platform tools rot. First a runtime check creeps in — if wasm, do this, else do that. Then it breeds. Then a mock layer. Then, quietly, a second lite build with its own bugs… and within a year you maintain two programs wearing one name. [curious] So the same binary everywhere reads like marketing. This page is the receipt. The whole fork — every difference between the two targets — is one trait… five methods… one file. And here's the trick. The compiler picks the side. Not an if-statement.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. The seam is the single trait — called Io, with five capability methods — where the wbx CLI's two compile targets are allowed to differ. Everything above it — arg parsing, kernel calls, the JSON envelopes — is target-blind. Below it… native uses the standard library and reqwest; wasm uses host imports, brokered by the runtime Dock. [excited] And the best part — the thesis is written at the top of the file itself, word for word. The capability seam. The only place native and wasm targets differ. Below it, native uses standard library and reqwest; wasm uses host imports brokered by the Dock — capabilities granted… not assumed. That last clause is the whole design in four words. You don't abstract the platform. You abstract the capabilities — the short list of things the CLI ever asks the outside world for.

tracks.title: Five questions, one vocabulary
tracks.text: Five questions, one vocabulary. The entire list of things the CLI asks the world for is five methods. First… http — a request to the discovered engine. And notice — the argument is path-only. No host. Where the engine lives isn't the caller's business; discovery supplies it. Second… http url — the same verb, but for an arbitrary full address, like a self-hosted publish target. Third… read — bytes at a path. Fourth… write — bytes to a path. And fifth… spawn — run a program, return its output. That's how deploy reaches docker and krunvm; how publish reaches wrangler and git. Now, which verb touches which capability? Picture a small table. The kernel verbs — query, lint, tangle — bottom out in read, because the kernel is linked right in. The engine verbs — build, run, library — ride on http. Deploy reaches for spawn, plus read and write. And publish needs spawn plus http url. [curious] The verdict, in one line — kernel verbs land on read, engine verbs on http, and only the heavy orchestration verbs reach for spawn. There is no sixth row… because there is no sixth capability.

tracks.title: The compiler is the switch
tracks.text: The compiler is the switch. So which implementation of the trait do you get? A function called platform decides — and it decides at compile time, keyed on the target triple. Picture the code. There's the trait — http, http url, read, write, spawn. Then platform, which says — if not wasm, hand back the Native implementation; if wasm, hand back the Wasm one. The consequence is the entire point. Every line above the seam holds a generic Io handle and cannot tell which target it's on. The function that makes RCP calls is one line — it just calls http. No branching on platform. No asking… am I in a sandbox. The compiler already answered. And the proof this is real lives in the dependency list. reqwest — the HTTP client — is a target-gated dependency. One line in the build manifest says — only compile reqwest when the target is not wasm. So the wasm build never even contains a socket client. [excited] Two commands make the two artifacts. Cargo build release gives you native wbx. Cargo build release, target wasm thirty-two wasi-p-one, gives you wbx dot wasm. Picture the flow as a diagram. One source flows down into cargo, which forks on exactly one thing — the target triple. The native branch yields an implementation on the standard library and reqwest, with the operating system's ambient authority. The wasm branch yields one on WASI preopens and Dock host imports, where nothing is assumed and everything is granted. The fork has one node… and it's the compiler. Why Rust, and not the project's Elixir tool? Because the binary must run three places — a laptop with no Erlang, inside the runtime, and inside the wasm sandbox. An Elixir tool fails the first and the third. It drags the whole BEAM and can't compile to wasm.

tracks.title: Finding the engine — runtime dot json
tracks.text: Finding the engine. The http method dials the discovered engine — and here's the surprise. Where the engine lives is itself a capability… and that capability is a small JSON file. The runtime writes it; the CLI reads it; the path is canon on both sides. Picture the file. It holds a port — four thousand. A token — twenty-four random bytes. A process id. A scheme — http. And a mode — container. It's written to a disco folder under the app-data directory… and it's locked to mode six hundred — owner read-write only — because that token is a local credential. Now picture the round trip as a sequence. You run wbx deploy local. The CLI spawns a container, bind-mounting a slash-disco folder to the real app-data folder on your machine. Inside, the runtime boots on port four thousand, mints a fresh token, and writes runtime dot json at mode six hundred. That write lands — through the bind mount — in the exact host folder the native CLI reads from. So next time you run any engine verb, wbx finds the file, reads scheme, port and token, and dials one-twenty-seven-oh-oh-one on port four thousand… with a bearer header. [excited] Two processes… no shared library… one agreed-upon path. That's discovery. And there's one escape hatch, before discovery even runs. Set the engine URL environment variable, and the CLI skips the file entirely — because that file only knows about local engines. A remote one, you name directly.

tracks.title: The native edge, end to end
tracks.text: The native edge, end to end. Let's trace one verb on a laptop. You type wbx library. Above the seam, the verb builds a request for the path slash-api-slash-library-slash-local, and hands it down. On native, four things happen in order. First… the remote override — if the engine URL is set, use it and skip discovery. Second… discovery runs — read runtime dot json, parse scheme, port and token; a missing port is the only hard error. Third… the URL is assembled — scheme, loopback, port, path — with a bearer header, added only when the token isn't empty. And fourth… a fresh blocking client makes the call. Only GET, POST, PUT and DELETE are allowed; a body forces JSON content type; a non-success status becomes an error carrying the status and the body. Now — what if the discovery file isn't there? The error is canon, and it reads like this. No runtime discovery at that path — is the runtime running — try wbx deploy local. [curious] And that string does more than apologize. The exit-code map sees the words runtime dot json and classifies it as code three — engine unreachable, marked retryable, with a hint to start one or set the engine URL. So a missing file isn't a stack trace. It's a typed, retryable, fix-it-yourself condition an agent can branch on without reading prose.

tracks.title: The wasm edge — granted, not assumed
tracks.text: The wasm edge — granted, not assumed. Compile the same trait for wasm, and here's the most surprising fact. Read and write are the exact same standard-library code as native. Not a shim — the identical lines. They work in the sandbox because WASI preopens hand the program real, capability-scoped file access. So the same call means two things — on native it's ambient OS authority; on wasm it's a granted preopen. Same shape, two authorities. Which is why the kernel and assembly verbs — query, tangle, lint, bundle — run fully in the sandbox. All they need from the world is to read a file. But http and spawn part ways. They don't pretend — they bail with a message that teaches. Engine verbs aren't available in the wasm sandbox yet — the Dock HTTP broker is pending — run the native wb. Picture the five methods across three columns — native, wasm today, and wasm intended. Read and write are green in all three — they work now. Http and http url work natively, bail today, and arrive later as Dock host imports. And spawn works natively and stays native-only — by design. [curious] The verdict — two methods already work identically because file IO is a WASI primitive; two wait on the Dock; and spawn stays native, because orchestrating containers from inside a sandbox is not a thing the sandbox should do. And the pattern that pending http will follow already exists today — the Rust Dock provides host functions, like host http get and host exec, each policy-gated by profile, with a sixty-four-request ceiling. When the broker lands, the wasm http becomes exactly that — a host call the runtime can deny — not a socket the CLI opens. Capabilities granted… not assumed.

tracks.title: The two other cfg sites
tracks.text: The two other config sites. If the seam is the only place targets differ, why does wbx dev act differently in the sandbox? Because the seam stays one file by letting a few verbs declare themselves native at the verb — instead of leaking config blocks everywhere. There are exactly two such satellites — verified by grep, the whole fork is three files. First… wbx dev. It serves a local preview — interactive, long-running, polling file times every three hundred milliseconds and binding a socket to inject a reload. None of that belongs in a sandbox, so the wasm build bails — wbx dev needs the native binary; in-sandbox, use wbx bundle. Second… the interactive picker. Its wasm version returns the default silently, so the sandboxed CLI can never block on input waiting for a person who isn't there. [curious] Both express one discipline — a verb that's inherently interactive or long-running owns its own config at the point of use… and the seam itself stays the single capability boundary it claims to be.

tracks.title: One path, two languages
tracks.text: One path, two languages. The discovery path lives twice — once in Elixir, once in Rust. And that duplication is correct… not drift. Two separate processes, two languages, no shared library — they must agree on one file location. So each computes it, and the comments cross-reference to keep them honest. Read the two side by side. The Rust version — a desktop-dir override points at runtime dot json; otherwise the app-dir slash disco slash runtime dot json; and the app dir is the Application Support folder on macOS, or dot-local-share elsewhere. The Elixir version — same override, same per-OS roots, same filename. The Elixir comment says it outright — the path is canon on both sides, so raw-dev and container runtimes are discovered identically. The duplication is the honest cost of having two processes meet at a file instead of through a shared binary — and the cross-referencing comments are how the project polices the drift that duplication invites. One detail to carry — every environment variable here has two spellings. The CLI tries the W-B-X prefix first, then falls back to the legacy W-B one.

tracks.title: What bails today
tracks.text: The honest part — what bails today. The in-sandbox wbx is partial right now. And the choice worth defending is that it fails loudly, with the fix in the message, instead of pretending. Picture the real line. First… works in the sandbox today — query, tangle, lint, bundle, unbundle, sign and verify; they need only file IO, and preopens grant it. Second… bails in the sandbox — the engine verbs like build, run and library; the Dock HTTP broker is pending. Third… also bails — publish and deploy; spawn is native-only orchestration. And fourth… native-only — dev, because it's interactive and binds a socket. Three caveats sit beside that. The Dock broker for the CLI is pending — not shipped; no runtime module references wbx dot wasm today, so in-sandbox docking is genuinely not wired yet. The runtime image bakes the CLI so container agents use the same tool users do — but those agents run the native linux build, not the wasm one. And the wasm artifact does ship — from CI, on every release tag, built for the wasi target, into one GitHub release. [curious] The wasm side is real, shipped, and downloadable — it just doesn't yet have the Dock socket it will eventually dial through. Telling you that… is the contract.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. Why a trait object — not feature flags or two crates? Because a trait object lets every verb hold one generic handle and stay target-blind, while the compiler picks the concrete side. Feature flags would compile both worlds and gate them with conditionals that spread; two crates would be the second lite build this whole design exists to avoid. Why does wasm read-write work, but http doesn't? Because file IO is a WASI primitive and sockets aren't — by design. Preopens give scoped file access for free; outbound network has to be brokered by the host. Is the discovery token a secret? Yes — twenty-four random bytes, minted per boot, written at mode six hundred, required on every engine call. Treat it like any key on your machine. What if I run the engine remotely? Set the engine URL — and the token, if it needs auth — and the CLI skips discovery and dials that address. And — W-B-X or W-B for the variables? [chuckles] Both. The CLI tries the W-B-X spelling first, then the legacy W-B one.

tracks.title: Back up to wbx
tracks.text: So that's the seam. The whole difference between two build targets, drawn in one file, picked by the compiler — five methods, one vocabulary, and a rule that the difference never leaks past them. You don't abstract the platform… you abstract the capabilities. [curious] If you want the bigger frame — one crate, two targets, the agents holding the same tool you do — that's the parent lesson, wbx. Lesson seven. Go read it next. Everything here was just the receipt for the claim it makes.
